reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because the speaker urges invitations and activation of increasingly expensive levels, with rewards flowing to an activated upline partner. The meeting claims first-cycle income can fund another upgrade and warns that limited activation may restrict earnings or result in lost money when team members overtake a participant. The transcript and frames do not establish completed payments, actual losses, or independently verified reward outcomes.

citations.quote: Upgrade is the activation of the next, more expensive level.
we need to invite people every day
pushing them level because this opportunity more bigger level more income
when your partner or downline or anyone, when you activate your level then it gets a position
then you can get reward

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker does not present the reward discussion as a verified account of what participants have earned. He says the current figures are unusual, asks leaders why newcomers stop at early levels, and discusses a possible response. His warning about limited earnings is conditional on activating only two levels, not evidence that a viewer has suffered a loss. Read the meeting as leaders questioning participant behavior and explaining program rules, not as proof of a deceptive payoff.

citations.quote: our developers already checked the stats and the stats are unusual.
Maybe you know the reason and you can explain to me.
if you activate only two levels in X-Core, of course you will always be limited in your earnings

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's quotes establish that the speaker describes costly levels, invitations and potential rewards. They do not establish that any stated income was paid, that an upgrade produced a return, or that the speaker concealed uncertainty. Indeed, the same discussion asks leaders to explain why newcomers are not advancing.

citations.quote: Why aren't you pushing them to activate more expensive levels? Maybe you know the reason and you can explain to me.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Uncertainty about actual payouts does not remove the promotional mechanism. The speaker explicitly asks leaders to push newcomers toward more expensive levels, describes first-cycle income as sufficient for the next upgrade, and says an upgrade reward goes to an activated upline. Those are claims about how participants should advance and how rewards flow, regardless of whether completed payments are independently verified.

citations.quote: Why aren't you pushing them to activate more expensive levels?
Income from first cycle of each level is enough to upgrade to the next level. The reward for the upgrade goes to your upline partner

opening.argument: Judge, this is framed as an ambassador meeting with a knowledge test. The speaker asks participants where rewards go when a level freezes and whether someone can overtake an upline partner; later, a participant asks how to tell where rewards go. That question-and-answer structure matters. It supports reading the disputed statements as an explanation of program mechanics for existing leaders, rather than a direct appeal to viewers to join or transfer money.

citations.quote: Ambassador program meeting with Eddy
Let's go straight to the test.
Where will the rewards go when your level is frozen?
How can we tell where our rewards goes?

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution identifies language about invitations and higher levels, but its reading leaves out the format in which that language appears. The speaker addresses people he calls priority leaders, tests their understanding, and takes a participant's question about placement. Explaining those mechanics in a meeting is not, by itself, evidence of a direct solicitation to the viewer.

citations.quote: Because I guess you guys are priority leaders so you should know. And if still not, let's just check it here, check yourself.
my question is that when we activate levels, our team partners, with our team so our rewards do not go to a client, it goes to teams or other teams.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A teaching format does not make the content merely neutral instruction. In the same meeting, the speaker asks leaders why they are not pushing newcomers to activate more expensive levels and proposes meetings and training to move them along. The test explains a reward structure involving upgrades and upline partners; the later discussion tells leaders to encourage participation in it.

citations.quote: Why aren't you pushing them to activate more expensive levels?
maybe those people should bring them to our meetings to our trainings
The reward for the upgrade goes to your upline partner provided that they already have this level activated

opening.argument: Judge, the record shows an ambassador program discussing tasks, meetings and level activation, but it does not show a viewer being asked for credentials, given a payment address, or promised a fixed return. The speaker even describes rewards as dependent on an upline partner already having a level activated. The safer conclusion from these excerpts is that participants are discussing the operation of a referral activity; the record does not independently establish a fraudulent transaction or its outcome.

citations.quote: I already added new tasks related to recording a video.
tomorrow's meetup with ambassadors, you need to make a full recording and it will be the claim.
The reward for the upgrade goes to your upline partner provided that they already have this level activated

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's evidence describes a referral and upgrade structure, but it does not document a completed payment or loss. Even its reward quote makes receipt contingent on an activated level. Those limits matter when moving from a description of a program's rules to a conclusion about what actually happened to participants.

citations.quote: The reward for the upgrade goes to your upline partner provided that they already have this level activated

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The concern is not limited to proving a completed loss, a credential request, or a fixed return. The meeting describes increasingly expensive activations, rewards passing to an upline partner, and earnings tied to a participant's team and levels. It also urges leaders to invite newcomers and push them toward higher levels. Calling that ordinary referral activity overlooks the tiered reward mechanism the speakers themselves describe.
